body.text: In short:
A popular Bluey-themed float was absent from Mount Gambier's annual Christmas parade after an infringement notice from the BBC.
The local real estate business said it was "disappointed" but respected the request.
What's next?
The BBC said unlicensed and unofficial activity risked diluting the goodwill.
A small business has been ordered by the BBC to remove its Bluey float from Mount Gambier's Christmas parade, citing a copyright infringement.

The BBC's Bluey Brand Protection Team sent a letter to The Property Co. SA, a family-owned real estate business in South Australia's south-east, over its award-winning float ahead of the weekend's festivities.
Principal and sales agent Bianca Taylor said this year was meant to be the third for the float, which consisted of the Heeler family's iconic house and three professionally made costumes.
The miniature house, made to resemble the yellow Queenslander from the ABC Kids TV show, was built "from scratch" and cost more than $8,000, Ms Taylor said.

"We received an email with a letter attached from the BBC over in London … and they've asked us to cease those operations or that activity with the local parade and to remove all marketing or any photos or anything at all," she said.
"We were extremely disappointed because we'd had such an amazing response from the community."

Ms Taylor said she had asked the BBC if there was an opportunity to have "a bit more of a conversation" about what other options were, but the broadcaster said it was not in a position to chat about licensing opportunities.
BBC confirms action
The BBC in a statement confirmed that BBC Studios issued a cease-and-desist letter in relation to this unlicensed Bluey event in December 2025.
"Our cease and desist letters do not seek to prevent events from taking place but rather request that any Bluey branding and references are removed," the statement said.
"We also make clear that, should event organisers wish to feature Bluey mascots, they are welcome to contact our official partners, whose details we can provide upon request."

The BBC said unlicensed and unofficial activity risked diluting the goodwill that shows like Bluey had built with their fans and audiences over a period of time and as brand custodians it would always take the necessary measures to mitigate any negative impact.
"This is particularly important when it comes to children's shows," the statement said.
BBC protecting the 'Bluey brand'

The senior lecturer from the University of New England said the "Bluey brand" as we know it was not just the name, it was the character design, the visual elements and drawings, which were all trademarked and protected by copyright.
"They're looking at quality control, and they're looking at [protecting] the trust that families have in the character … and they're asserting their rights because of that," Dr Potter said.
"[By] using the Bluey image and trademarks and dressing up, they are actually exercising other people's rights … if permission has not been sought or a license has not been paid for it."
Bluey was created by Queensland-based Ludo Studio, which owns the intellectual property (IP), while BBC Studios is the content's distributor.
Dr Potter's advice to organisations wanting to use images that were subject to copyright was to seek permission in advance.

"For the future, if any of these floats are looking at using very famous characters and licensed characters, they should seek permission just to avoid any problems … That would be the safest option," Dr Potter said.
"It's less likely that the rights holders would assert their rights if it was not associated with a commercial branch, but they still have the exact same equal rights to assert it either way.
"So, if a parent has gone to a shop and has bought a licensed costume, then that's been basically OK through intellectual property.

"But if a parent just sort of put together a homemade costume, then that's actually not a licensed costume, so technically in the eyes of the law, the rights holder could go after somebody for a non-licensed costume."
Community backing

Ms Taylor said it had been confusing to get an infringement notice for using Bluey in the float when other businesses and organisations were able to use characters which were also subject to copyright laws.
She said the community had been equally disappointed by the decision to not have the float in the 2026 parade.

"[On the day of the parade] I would have had 30 people, easily, just stop and want to chat about the situation which is overwhelming but positive that we've got such a backing from the community, I guess, but they are equally as disappointed."
It is the second time a Bluey-related controversy has made headlines in Mount Gambier. Last month, One Nation distributed colouring books at the local show depicting Bluey being held at knifepoint.
